stated: Support changing the law on assisted dying to allow people to choose to end their lives to avoid prolonging unnecessary suffering, provided it is their clear and settled will and proper safeguards are in place.

source.quote: Elected Greens will back changing the law on assisted dying. We support a humane and dignified approach to terminal illness, allowing people to choose to end their lives to avoid prolonging unnecessary suffering, if this is their clear and settled will. Proper safeguards would need to be put in place.

bearing_set.reason: The policy is fundamentally about the legal right to bodily autonomy and a dignified death; the safeguards clause directly invokes due process protections — both squarely within civil liberties and due-process scope.

Assisted dying would be administered through the healthcare system, changing the scope of end-of-life care available, with real implications for clinical roles, palliative care resourcing, and what 'treatment' means at end of life.

The policy primarily affects people in the final stages of life; it alters social care access and cost (an O8 indicator) by providing an alternative to prolonged end-of-life care, and raises non-negligible concerns about whether elderly or disabled people may face pressure to choose death — directly bearing on 'security against later-life poverty' and dignified care in old age.

The policy's core effect is removing a legal prohibition on an individual's choice over their own death, directly expanding bodily autonomy and freedom from state coercion — the defining O10 indicator.

membership_note: The policy is primarily a bodily-autonomy measure (O10 improves) with a genuine and contested equal-treatment/minority-protection dimension (O9 mixed). It does not materially move housing, healthcare capacity, wages, pensions, public finances, environment, or the other fundamentals through a specific, traceable mechanism.
